To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) HIV-specific IgG antibodies are transmitted to children born to HIV-infected mothers and may be detectable for up to 28 weeks; 2) HIV-specific IgM antibodies are not transmitted and are detectable only in HIV-infected infants; 3) HIV-specific IgA antibodies are not detectable in children born to HIV-positive mothers; and 4) HIV-specific IgE antibodies are detectable in children with symptomatic HIV infection, but are not a useful tool for
the detection of IgG3 antibodies against HIV in children born to HIV-positive mothers may help identify those children who will become HIV-infected.
the presence of HIV-specific IgG antibodies in the first year of the child of a seropositive mother indicates HIV-infection and their disappearance indicates that the child will not be infected.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the early diagnosis of HIV in children born to HIV-infected mothers.
the early diagnosis of HIV in the newborn child.
the early diagnosis of HIV in children.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIV-specific IgG1, IgG2 and IgG4 are transmitted to the child transplacentally, whereas HIV-specific IgG 3 is not.
the presence of specific IgG3 antibodies in the first year of the child born to HIV-infected mothers is a marker of HIV infection.
the persistence of IgG3 antibodies in a child of HIV-infected mother is indicative of HIV infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the clearance of HIV-specific IgG 3 in the first year of age heralds sero-conversion in uninfected children born to HIV-infected mothers.
the detection of IgG3 antibodies specific for HIV in the serum of children born to HIV-positive mothers can be a marker for early detection of HIV infection.
HIV-specific-Ig G3 antibodies are detectable in 75% of children born to HIV-infected mothers, in 100% of HIV-infected and in none of the uninfected children.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the detection of HIV-specific IgG1, IgG2, and IgG3 in children of HIV-seroposive mothers can help to diagnose HIV infection in children, and that the clearance of these antibodies can herald seroconversion in passive antibody-carrier infants.
the presence of IgG3 antibodies in children born to mothers with HIV can indicate the presence of the disease.
the detection of HIV-specific IgG1 and IgG3 antibodies in the serum of children born to HIV-infected mothers is an effective tool for the early diagnosis of HIV-infected infants.
